subject: Biology
title: Sex-Linked Traits
description: A quick, practical guide to Sex-Linked Traits.

hook.text: Some traits ride on the X chromosome. Males, with only one X, feel their effects more often.

buildup.text: Color blindness and hemophilia are X-linked recessive conditions carried mostly by females.

discovery.text: A mother can carry the gene without symptoms and pass it to her sons, who show the trait.

twist.text: Queen Victoria carried hemophilia and spread it across European royal families.

climax.text: Males need just one copy of an X-linked recessive allele to be affected. Females need two.

punchline.text: One X chromosome means nowhere to hide.

quiz.question: Why are males more often affected by X-linked recessive traits?
options: They have only one X chromosome
They inherit two copies more often

details.summary: Sex-linked traits are controlled by genes on the X or Y chromosome. Because males have only one X chromosome, recessive X-linked conditions like color blindness and hemophilia affect males far more frequently while females are usually unaffected carriers.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding sex-linked inheritance explains why certain genetic conditions disproportionately affect males and helps predict inheritance patterns in families with known carriers of X-linked disorders.
takeaways: Males express X-linked recessive traits from a single allele copy
Females need two copies of a recessive X-linked allele to be affected
Color blindness and hemophilia are classic X-linked recessive conditions

faq.question: Why are males more affected by X-linked disorders?
faq.answer: Males have one X and one Y chromosome. If their single X carries a recessive disease allele, they express the condition because there is no second X to compensate. Females with one affected X typically have a normal allele on their other X providing protection.

faq.question: Can fathers pass X-linked conditions to their sons?
faq.answer: No. Fathers pass their Y chromosome to sons and their X to daughters. X-linked conditions in males always come from the mother's X. A father with hemophilia passes his affected X only to daughters, who become carriers.
